life-why-physics-everyday.title: Why does everyday physics work?
life-why-physics-everyday.description: Curiosity library on static, magnets, ice, pressure, microwaves, mirrors and echoes.

courses.title: Static shocks, magnets and floating ice
courses.summary: Why you get a zap from a door handle, how magnets work, and why ice floats.
outcomes: Explain static electricity and discharge
Describe magnetic poles, domains and Earth's field
Explain why ice is less dense than water
Test ideas at home

scenes.text: Veda shuffles across the carpet in socks.
She touches the metal handle and feels a sharp snap.
Where did the electricity come from?

steps.title: Triboelectric charging
steps.body: When two different materials rub and separate, electrons move from one surface to the other. Your body can end up with excess negative or positive charge.

steps.title: The spark
steps.body: Charged you and the neutral handle form a strong electric field in the air gap. When the field exceeds roughly 3 million volts per metre (dry air), air breaks down and a spark jumps. The voltage can be thousands of volts, but the charge is tiny so the shock is harmless.

steps.title: Dry weather
steps.body: Humid air lets charge leak away, so shocks are more common in dry winter air.

steps.title: Reduce
steps.body: Touch metal with a key first, use cotton clothes, or add humidity.

steps.title: Safety
steps.body: Static from clothing is harmless, but mains electricity is dangerous; never test with sockets.

statements.s: Static shock is caused by charge transferred by rubbing.
The shock has high current so it is dangerous.
statements.why: Voltage is high but charge is tiny.

statements.s: Dry air makes static shocks more common.
Static electricity is the same as current from a socket.

quiz.q: What moves when you rub two materials?
Why are shocks common in winter?
Breakdown field of dry air is about...

scenes.text: Ayaan sticks a magnet to the fridge.
He cuts a bar magnet in two and gets two magnets.
His compass needle points north.

steps.title: Where magnetism comes from
steps.body: Moving electric charge produces magnetism. In atoms, electrons have spin and orbital motion that behave like tiny magnets. In iron, cobalt and nickel, groups of atoms line up in regions called **domains**; a magnet has most domains aligned.

steps.title: Poles
steps.body: Every magnet has north and south poles. Like poles repel, unlike attract. Cut a magnet in two and you get two smaller magnets; isolated monopoles have never been found.

steps.title: Earth
steps.body: Earth has a magnetic field generated by moving molten iron in the outer core. A compass needle aligns with it. The geographic north pole region is near Earth's magnetic south pole.

steps.title: Safe use
steps.body: Keep strong magnets away from small children, credit cards and pacemakers; swallowed magnets can be dangerous.

steps.title: Try
steps.body: Magnetise a needle by stroking it in one direction with a magnet and float it on water on a leaf.

statements.s: Cutting a magnet gives a separate north pole and south pole.
Like poles repel.
Earth has a magnetic field.
statements.why: It is made by the liquid outer core.

statements.s: All metals are attracted to magnets.
statements.why: Aluminium, copper are not attracted strongly.

quiz.q: Cut a bar magnet in half...
options: Two magnets each with N and S

scenes.text: Anika drops ice in a glass of water.
It floats with a small part above.
Most solids sink in their own liquid, so why not ice?

steps.title: Hydrogen bonds
steps.body: Water molecules form hydrogen bonds. In ice they lock into an open hexagonal lattice with more empty space, so ice expands by about 9% when it freezes.

steps.title: Density
steps.body: Ice is about 0.917 g/cm³ and water about 1.00 g/cm³ near 4 °C, so about 91.7% of a floating ice cube is below the surface (Archimedes).

steps.title: Why it matters
steps.body: Lakes freeze from the top down, insulating the water below so fish survive. Water is densest at about 4 °C.

steps.title: Burst pipes
steps.body: Freezing water expands and can burst pipes or bottles; do not freeze sealed glass.

steps.title: Try
steps.body: Float an ice cube in water and mark the line. Compare floating in salt water.

statements.s: Ice is denser than liquid water.
Water is densest at about 4 °C.
Most of a floating ice cube is underwater.
Lakes freeze from the bottom up.

quiz.q: Why do fish survive in frozen lakes?

courses.title: Pressure cookers, microwaves, mirrors and echoes
courses.summary: Everyday heat, wave and pressure devices: why a pressure cooker cooks faster, how microwaves heat food, how mirrors form images and why echoes happen.
outcomes: Explain boiling point and pressure
Explain microwave heating and safety
Explain reflection and mirror images
Calculate echo distances

scenes.text: Mummy cooks dal in a pressure cooker.
The weight on top whistles.
It cooks much faster than an open pot.

steps.title: Boiling point and pressure
steps.body: Water boils when its vapour pressure equals the pressure above it. In a sealed cooker, steam raises the pressure above atmospheric. At about 100 kPa above atmospheric, water boils near 120 °C instead of 100 °C.

steps.title: Faster cooking
steps.body: Cooking reactions speed up at higher temperature, so food cooks faster and uses less fuel. At high altitude, where air pressure is lower, water boils below 100 °C so a cooker is especially helpful.

steps.title: Safety valve
steps.body: A weight (regulator) lets steam out when pressure reaches a set value and a safety plug releases it in an emergency.

steps.title: Safety
steps.body: Never open the lid until pressure has dropped. Keep the vent clean and replace worn gaskets.

steps.title: Not exactly 120
steps.body: Real cookers vary; many reach roughly 115–121 °C.

statements.s: Higher pressure raises the boiling point of water.
A pressure cooker works by making food hotter than 100 °C.
You can open a hot pressurised cooker anytime.
Water always boils at 100 °C.

quiz.q: Water boils at about what temperature at ~2 atm absolute?

scenes.text: Sam reheats rice and the edges are hot but the middle cold.
He wonders if food becomes radioactive.
It does not.

steps.title: How it heats
steps.body: Domestic ovens use microwaves of about 2.45 GHz. Water, fats and sugars are polar, so the oscillating field makes them rotate and jostle; this friction between molecules heats the food (dielectric heating).

steps.title: Penetration
steps.body: Microwaves penetrate only a few centimetres, so deeper parts heat by conduction. Turntables and standing time even out hot spots.

steps.title: Safety
steps.body: Do not run empty; no metal foil or sealed containers; stir liquids, since superheating can cause sudden boiling. Food is not made radioactive.

steps.title: Even heating
steps.body: Cover loosely, stir, rest.

steps.title: Not ionising
steps.body: Microwaves are non-ionising and do not alter atoms.

statements.s: Microwaved food becomes radioactive.
Microwaves mainly heat water molecules.
Metal foil is safe in microwaves.
A turntable helps with hot spots.
statements.why: It moves food through the pattern.

story.title: Hall of mirrors and a well

scenes.text: Tara raises her right hand and her reflection raises its 'right' hand.
At a deep well she shouts and hears her voice return.
Both are reflection: of light and of sound.

steps.title: Law of reflection
steps.body: The angle of incidence equals the angle of reflection. A plane mirror forms a virtual image the same size as the object, as far behind the mirror as you are in front.

steps.title: Why not left-right flipped?
steps.body: A mirror reverses front to back, not left to right. We see an image that looks flipped because we imagine turning ourselves around.

steps.title: Echo
steps.body: An echo is reflected sound. To hear it distinct from the original, the delay must be at least about 0.1 s. With sound at 343 m/s, the round trip of 34.3 m means the reflecting surface should be at least about 17 m away.

steps.title: Depth
steps.body: If an echo from a well returns after 0.6 s: distance = 343 × 0.6 / 2 ≈ 103 m (for a very deep shaft).

steps.title: Reverberation
steps.body: In small rooms reflections overlap, so you hear reverberation instead of echo.

statements.s: A plane mirror image is smaller than the object.
An echo is reflected sound.
The minimum distance for a clear echo is about 17 m.
A mirror flips left and right.

quiz.q: Minimum reflector distance for a clear echo?
Image in a plane mirror is...

lessons.title: Lab: Capstone – echo and mirror measurements

scenes.text: A class stands facing a tall wall.
They clap and time the echo.
Then test two mirrors at an angle.

steps.title: Echo method
steps.body: Stand about 40 m from a wall, clap and time 10 clap-echo intervals with a stopwatch. Divide to get the time, then distance = 343 × t / 2.

steps.title: Mirrors
steps.body: Place two mirrors at 90° and count the images of a coin.

steps.title: Safety
steps.body: Do not do loud claps near people's ears.

steps.title: Compare
steps.body: Compare your measured distance with a tape measure.

life-why-sleep-brain.title: Why do we sleep, dream and remember?
life-why-sleep-brain.description: Curiosity library on sleep and memory: stages, oddities, forgetting, déjà vu and jet lag. Educational only; not medical advice.

courses.title: Sleepwalking, dreams, nightmares and sleep paralysis
courses.summary: What happens in the sleeping brain: sleep stages, sleepwalking and sleep talking, dreams and nightmares, sleep paralysis and the falling feeling.
outcomes: Describe NREM and REM sleep
Explain why sleepwalking and sleep talking occur
Explain sleep paralysis and hypnic jerks calmly
Keep a sleep and dream diary

scenes.text: Nina's mother finds her walking in the hall at 1 a.m., eyes open.
Next morning Nina remembers nothing.
Part of her brain was awake enough to move, but not enough to remember.

steps.title: Learning, not medical advice
steps.body: This is for learning, not medical advice. For your own health, talk to a doctor or pharmacist. In an emergency call 112.

steps.title: Sleep stages
steps.body: Sleep cycles through light and deep **NREM** sleep and **REM** sleep about every 90 minutes. Deep NREM sleep is more common early in the night.

steps.title: Sleepwalking
steps.body: Sleepwalking and sleep talking are partial arousals from deep NREM sleep: movement systems wake while conscious awareness and memory stay asleep. They are more common in children and often run in families.

steps.title: Safety
steps.body: Gently guide a sleepwalker back to bed; do not shout. Lock outside doors, keep stairs and sharp objects safe.

steps.title: See a doctor if
steps.body: episodes are frequent, violent, start in adulthood, or cause injury.

steps.title: Triggers
steps.body: Sleep deprivation, fever, stress and an irregular schedule increase episodes.

statements.s: It is dangerous to wake a sleepwalker.
statements.why: Waking is not harmful, but guiding is gentler and may confuse them.

statements.s: Sleepwalking mostly arises from deep non-REM sleep.
Sleep talking means the person is telling the truth.
statements.why: Content is often jumbled and unreliable.

statements.s: Lack of sleep can increase sleepwalking.

quiz.why: It is a partial arousal from deep NREM sleep.

quiz.q: How should you help a sleepwalker?
options: Guide them gently back to bed
quiz.why: Calm guidance and a safe home help.
Lack of sleep is a trigger.

quiz.q: About how long is a sleep cycle?

scenes.text: Imran dreams he arrives for an exam with no pen.
He wakes with a racing heart.
By breakfast it feels silly, but why did his brain make it?

steps.title: Learning, not medical advice
steps.body: This is for learning, not medical advice. For your own health, talk to a doctor or pharmacist. In an emergency call 112.

steps.title: REM sleep
steps.body: Vivid dreams occur mostly in **REM** sleep, when the brain is highly active, eye movements are rapid and most voluntary muscles are paralysed (REM atonia), which stops us acting out dreams.

steps.title: Why dream?
steps.body: Theories include memory consolidation, emotional processing and random activation woven into stories by the cortex. Scientists do not agree on one answer; dream-reading books claiming fixed symbols have no scientific basis.

steps.title: Nightmares
steps.body: Nightmares are vivid disturbing dreams that wake you. They are common in childhood and with stress, trauma, irregular sleep or some medicines. Regular routines, calm evenings and talking about worries help.

steps.title: Get help
steps.body: If nightmares are frequent and distressing, speak to a doctor or counsellor. Tele-MANAS 14416 offers mental health support in India.

steps.title: Everyone dreams
steps.body: Most people dream several times a night even if they do not remember.

statements.s: Everyone dreams, even when they do not remember.
Dream dictionaries are scientifically proven.
statements.why: Meanings are personal and not fixed.

statements.s: Most vivid dreaming happens in REM sleep.
statements.why: Brain activity is high in REM.

statements.s: Nightmares only happen to children.

quiz.q: Which stage has the most vivid dreams?
quiz.why: REM is linked to vivid dreaming.

quiz.q: Why are muscles paralysed in REM?
options: To stop us acting out dreams

quiz.q: A helpful approach to frequent nightmares?
options: Regular sleep routine and seeking help

quiz.q: Do scientists agree on one purpose for dreams?

lessons.title: Sleep paralysis and the falling feeling

scenes.text: Sana wakes but cannot move for a minute and feels frightened.
She searches online and sees scary ghost stories.
A doctor explains it is a harmless mix-up of REM and waking.

steps.title: Learning, not medical advice
steps.body: This is for learning, not medical advice. For your own health, talk to a doctor or pharmacist. In an emergency call 112.

steps.title: Sleep paralysis
steps.body: During REM the brain keeps muscles relaxed. If awareness returns before this switches off, you are awake but unable to move for seconds to a couple of minutes. Hallucinated sensations can accompany it. It is common and harmless but frightening.

steps.title: Coping
steps.body: Remind yourself it will pass, try to wiggle fingers or toes, and keep a regular sleep schedule. Sleeping on your back and sleep deprivation make it more likely.

steps.title: Hypnic jerk
steps.body: The sudden 'falling' jolt as you drift off is a hypnic jerk: a brief muscle twitch, probably as muscles relax and the brain misreads it. It is normal.

steps.title: See a doctor
steps.body: If you also fall asleep suddenly in the day, seek advice, as it can occur in narcolepsy.

steps.title: Cultural stories
steps.body: Many cultures explain sleep paralysis as spirits; science explains it as a REM-wake overlap.

statements.s: Sleep paralysis is caused by a ghost sitting on your chest.
Hypnic jerks are normal.
statements.why: They are common when falling asleep.

statements.s: Sleep paralysis is dangerous and can stop breathing.
Regular sleep reduces sleep paralysis.

options: Awareness returns before REM paralysis ends
A brief twitch when falling asleep

quiz.q: Best coping step during sleep paralysis?
options: Stay calm and wiggle fingers or toes

steps.title: Hygiene

steps.title: Note
steps.body: If something in the diary worries you, share it with a doctor.

courses.title: Memory, déjà vu, forgetting and jet lag
courses.summary: How memory is built and lost, why déjà vu happens, why we forget, and how the body clock causes jet lag.
outcomes: Explain encoding, storage, retrieval
Describe leading theories of déjà vu
Explain forgetting and evidence-based study methods
Explain circadian rhythm and jet lag

scenes.text: Leela cannot remember where she parked.
Yet she recalls her school song word for word.
Memory is not one thing; it has stages.

steps.title: Learning, not medical advice
steps.body: This is for learning, not medical advice. For your own health, talk to a doctor or pharmacist. In an emergency call 112.

steps.title: Three stages
steps.body: **Encoding** takes in information, **storage** keeps it, and **retrieval** brings it back. Attention at encoding matters most: if you were not paying attention, nothing was stored.

steps.title: Types
steps.body: Working memory holds a few items for seconds. Long-term memory includes facts (semantic), personal events (episodic) and skills (procedural). The hippocampus is important for forming new episodic memories.

steps.title: Consolidation
steps.body: Sleep helps stabilise new memories, which is one reason all-night cramming often fails.

steps.title: Reconstructive
steps.body: Remembering rebuilds the memory each time, so memories can change and be wrong while feeling certain.

steps.title: Try
steps.body: Look at a list of 10 words for 30 seconds, then write as many as you recall.

statements.s: Memory works like a video recording.
statements.why: It is reconstructive and can distort.

statements.s: Sleep helps consolidate memories.
The hippocampus is important for forming new memories.
We only use 10 percent of the brain.
statements.why: This is a myth; imaging shows widespread use.

quiz.q: Which brain structure is key for new episodic memories?
Riding a bicycle is what type?
Why can confident memories be wrong?

lessons.title: Déjà vu and why we forget

scenes.text: On a trip to a new fort, Harsh feels he has been here before.
He never has.
He wonders if it's a past life. Science has other answers.

steps.title: Learning, not medical advice
steps.body: This is for learning, not medical advice. For your own health, talk to a doctor or pharmacist. In an emergency call 112.

steps.title: Déjà vu
steps.body: About two-thirds of people report experiencing déjà vu, often between teens and twenties. Leading hypotheses: the scene resembles a forgotten similar scene, or a brief glitch in memory-familiarity signals. It is not evidence of past lives or prediction.

steps.title: Epilepsy
steps.body: Frequent déjà vu with other symptoms in temporal lobe epilepsy is a reason to see a doctor, but occasional déjà vu is normal.

steps.title: Why we forget
steps.body: Forgetting is normal: information that is not retrieved fades, similar memories interfere, and retrieval cues are missing. Ebbinghaus found rapid forgetting soon after learning, then a slower decline.

steps.title: Study smart
steps.body: Space your practice over days, test yourself instead of just re-reading, and sleep well.

steps.title: Try
steps.body: Study 10 facts today, quiz yourself tomorrow and again in three days.

statements.s: Déjà vu proves you lived before.
statements.why: Memory-familiarity explanations are far better supported.

statements.s: Forgetting is a normal brain process.
Self-testing improves long-term retention.
Re-reading is the best way to learn.

quiz.q: Déjà vu is best explained as...
Which study method is best supported?
When should déjà vu be checked?

lessons.title: Jet lag and the body clock

scenes.text: Rohit flies from Delhi to London, 5.5 hours behind.
At 3 p.m. London time he is desperate to sleep.
His inner clock still says it is evening.

steps.title: Learning, not medical advice
steps.body: This is for learning, not medical advice. For your own health, talk to a doctor or pharmacist. In an emergency call 112.

steps.title: Circadian rhythm
steps.body: The suprachiasmatic nucleus in the hypothalamus is the master clock, running about 24 hours and reset mainly by light. It controls sleep timing, hormones such as melatonin, and body temperature.

steps.title: Jet lag
steps.body: Crossing time zones leaves the body clock out of step with local time. Symptoms: tiredness, poor concentration, appetite and gut changes. Flying east is usually harder than west because it requires advancing the clock.

steps.title: Reduce it
steps.body: Get daylight at local times, adjust sleep a little before travel, stay hydrated, and avoid excess caffeine and alcohol.

steps.title: Rule of thumb
steps.body: Adjustment is often cited as roughly one day per time zone crossed, though it varies.

steps.title: Shift work
steps.body: Long-term shift work also disrupts the clock; discuss health concerns with a doctor.

statements.s: Jet lag is worse flying east than west for most people.
Light is the main cue that resets the body clock.
statements.why: Light acts on the SCN via the eyes.

statements.s: Jet lag is imaginary.
statements.why: It is a real circadian mismatch.

statements.s: Melatonin is a hormone linked to sleep timing.

quiz.q: Where is the master body clock?

options: Body clock and local time mismatch

life-why-tech.title: How does my tech work?
life-why-tech.description: Curiosity library on phones, Wi-Fi, GPS, the internet, UPI, batteries and touchscreens.

courses.title: How phones, Wi-Fi and GPS work
courses.summary: Radio waves in everyday life: mobile networks, Wi-Fi, and how GPS finds your position.
outcomes: Explain cells, towers and handoff
Explain Wi-Fi bands and range
Explain GPS trilateration and clocks
Check your own signal and location safely

lessons.title: How a mobile phone call works

scenes.text: Ria calls her grandmother in another city.
Her voice goes by radio to a tower.
Then through fibre and exchanges to Nani's tower.

steps.title: Cells
steps.body: A mobile network divides land into **cells**, each served by a base station (tower). Your phone talks to the nearest tower on radio frequencies, then the network carries the call through wired backbones to the other tower.

steps.title: Handoff
steps.body: As you move, the network hands your connection to the next cell without dropping the call. Neighbouring cells use different frequencies to avoid interference, and frequencies are reused farther away.

steps.title: Digital voice
steps.body: Your voice is digitised, compressed and sent as data packets; modern calls (VoLTE) run over the 4G/5G data network. Your SIM identifies your subscription.

steps.title: Fact
steps.body: Radio waves are electromagnetic waves travelling at the speed of light, around 3 × 10⁸ m/s.

steps.title: Weak signal
steps.body: Walls and distance weaken signals; moving near a window can help.

statements.s: A phone connects directly to the other phone by radio.
statements.why: It goes via towers and the network.

statements.s: Handoff keeps calls going as you move.
Mobile radio waves travel at the speed of light.
Towers only cover whole countries.

options: An area served by a base station
Passing the call to the next tower

scenes.text: Dev studies near the router and the video is smooth.
In the far bedroom it buffers.
The radio signal is weaker there.

steps.title: Wi-Fi
steps.body: Wi-Fi is wireless local networking using radio, typically in the 2.4 GHz and 5 GHz bands (and 6 GHz in newer standards). Your router connects to the internet through your ISP and shares it with devices.

steps.title: Bands
steps.body: 2.4 GHz travels farther and passes walls better but is slower and crowded; 5 GHz is faster but has shorter range.

steps.title: Security
steps.body: Use WPA2 or WPA3 with a strong password. Public open Wi-Fi can be risky; use HTTPS sites and avoid sensitive tasks.

steps.title: Improve
steps.body: Place the router centrally and high, away from thick walls and metal.

steps.title: Not the internet itself
steps.body: Wi-Fi is only the last wireless hop; the internet is the wider network.

statements.s: Wi-Fi and the internet are the same thing.
statements.why: Wi-Fi is the local wireless link.

statements.s: 5 GHz usually has shorter range than 2.4 GHz.
An open public Wi-Fi is automatically safe.
WPA3 is more secure than old WEP.

scenes.text: Aman opens maps in an unfamiliar town.
His phone listens to satellites overhead.
A blue dot appears within a few metres.

steps.title: Satellites and clocks
steps.body: GPS satellites orbit at about 20,200 km and each broadcasts its position and the exact time from onboard atomic clocks. Your phone only receives; it does not send your location to the satellites.

steps.title: Trilateration
steps.body: Radio signals travel at the speed of light, so the delay tells your phone its distance from each satellite. Three distances fix a point; a fourth satellite corrects your phone's cheap clock. So at least four satellites are needed.

steps.title: Timing
steps.body: 20,200 km ÷ 3 × 10⁸ m/s ≈ 0.067 s (67 ms). A timing error of 1 microsecond gives a range error of about 300 m, so clock accuracy is vital.

steps.title: Relativity
steps.body: Relativity corrections are built into the system; without them errors would grow by kilometres per day.

steps.title: India
steps.body: India also has its own regional system, NavIC, and phones often use several systems together.

statements.s: Your phone sends your location to the GPS satellites.
At least four satellites are needed for position and time.
statements.why: Three for position plus one for the clock.

statements.s: GPS works by measuring signal travel time.
GPS satellites are in low Earth orbit like the ISS.

quiz.q: Satellites needed for a 3D fix plus clock?

courses.title: Internet, UPI, batteries and touchscreens
courses.summary: How the internet moves data, how UPI payments work, why batteries store energy and how touchscreens feel your finger.
outcomes: Explain packets, IP, DNS and HTTPS
Explain the UPI payment flow and safety
Calculate battery energy and explain Li-ion
Explain capacitive touchscreens

scenes.text: Meera video-calls her cousin abroad.
Her voice and video are cut into small packets.
Each packet finds its way across many routers.

steps.title: Packets
steps.body: Data is broken into small **packets**, each labelled with source and destination addresses. Routers forward each packet toward its destination; packets may take different routes and are reassembled at the end.

steps.title: IP and DNS
steps.body: Every device has an **IP address**. The **DNS** acts like a phone book, converting names like example.com into IP addresses.

steps.title: TCP and HTTPS
steps.body: TCP resends lost packets and keeps order; HTTPS encrypts web traffic using TLS so others on the path cannot read it.

steps.title: Cables
steps.body: Most international traffic travels through undersea fibre-optic cables, using pulses of light.

steps.title: Check
steps.body: Look for the padlock and a correct web address before entering passwords.

statements.s: The internet sends whole files as a single piece.
DNS converts names to IP addresses.
HTTPS encrypts web traffic.
Most international data goes by satellite.

scenes.text: Arjun scans a QR code at a tea stall.
He enters his UPI PIN.
In seconds the shopkeeper hears a confirmation.

steps.title: What UPI is
steps.body: Unified Payments Interface (UPI) is a real-time bank-to-bank payment system operated by NPCI (National Payments Corporation of India). Apps are interfaces; the money moves between bank accounts.

steps.title: Flow
steps.body: You scan a QR or enter a UPI ID (virtual payment address). The app sends a request to its bank; NPCI routes it to the receiver's bank; your bank checks your **UPI PIN**, debits and the other bank credits. Both sides get confirmations.

steps.title: Security
steps.body: Two factors: your registered device (SIM binding) and your PIN. You enter a PIN to pay, never to receive money.

steps.title: Fraud
steps.body: Never share your PIN or OTP. A 'collect request' to receive money is a scam sign. Report fraud to your bank and call 1930, India's cyber crime helpline.

steps.title: Anytime
steps.body: UPI works 24×7, including holidays.

statements.s: You need to enter your UPI PIN to receive money.
UPI moves money between bank accounts.
NPCI operates UPI.
Sharing the OTP with a caller is safe.

quiz.q: When do you enter the PIN?

scenes.text: Neha's phone dies at 3 p.m.
Her gloves do not work on the screen.
Both facts have clear physics.

steps.title: Li-ion battery
steps.body: During discharge lithium ions move from the graphite anode through an electrolyte to the cathode, while electrons flow through the phone, powering it. Charging reverses the movement.

steps.title: Energy
steps.body: Energy (Wh) = voltage × capacity (Ah). A 5000 mAh battery at 3.7 V holds 5 × 3.7 = 18.5 Wh.

steps.title: Safety
steps.body: Do not use damaged chargers or puncture batteries; heat and swelling are danger signs. Avoid leaving phones in hot cars.

steps.title: Capacitive touch
steps.body: The screen has a grid of electrodes storing small electric charge. A conductive finger changes the local capacitance; the controller detects where. Ordinary gloves insulate, so they fail unless conductive.

steps.title: Care
steps.body: Avoid always draining to 0%; moderate charge levels help lifespan.

statements.s: Li-ion charging reverses ion movement.
statements.why: Ions move back to the anode.

statements.s: Touchscreens detect pressure only.
5000 mAh at 3.7 V is 18.5 Wh.
Swollen batteries are fine to use.

steps.body: Do not write PINs or share screenshots with PINs.
